**Function extensionality.** If two functions return equal results for all possible arguments, then
they are equal.

It is called “extensionality” because it provides a way to prove two objects equal based on the
properties of the underlying mathematical functions, rather than based on the syntax used to denote
them.…

The relation `r` does not need to be an equivalence relation to use this axiom. When `r` is not an
equivalence relation, the quotient is with respect to the equivalence relation generated by `r`.

that the sequence is frequently in some bounded set.

**The axiom of choice**. `Nonempty α` is a proof that `α` has an element,
but the element itself is erased. The axiom `choice` supplies a particular
element of `α` given only this proof.

The textbook axiom of choice normally makes a family of choices all at once,

The natural numbers, starting at zero.

This type is special-cased by both the kernel and the compiler, and overridden with an efficient
implementation. Both use a fast arbitrary-precision arithmetic library (usually
[GMP](https://gmplib.org/)); at runtime, `Nat` values that are sufficiently small are unboxed.

A pseudometric space is a type endowed with a `ℝ`-valued distance `dist` satisfying
reflexivity `dist x x = 0`, commutativity `dist x y = dist y x`, and the triangle inequality
`dist x z ≤ dist x y + dist y z`.

Note that we do not require `dist x y = 0 → x = y`. See metric spaces (`MetricSpace`) for the
similar class…

Rational numbers, implemented as a pair of integers `num / den` such that the
denominator is positive and the numerator and denominator are coprime.
A pseudometric space is proper if all closed balls are compact.

The type `ℝ` of real numbers constructed as equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences of rational

Quotient types coarsen the propositional equality for a type so that terms related by some
equivalence relation are considered equal. The equivalence relation is given by an instance of
`Setoid`.

Set-theoretically, `Quotient s` can seen as the set of equivalence classes of `α` modulo the
`Setoid` instance's relation…

Low-level quotient types. Quotient types coarsen the propositional equality for a type `α`, so that
terms related by some relation `r` are considered equal in `Quot r`.

Set-theoretically, `Quot r` can be seen as the set of equivalence classes of `α` modulo `r`.
Functions from `Quot r` must prove that they respect `r`…

A setoid is a type with a distinguished equivalence relation, denoted `≈`.

The `Quotient` type constructor requires a `Setoid` instance.

A set is a collection of elements of some type `α`.

Although `Set` is defined as `α → Prop`, this is an implementation detail which should not be
relied on. Instead, `Set.ofPred` (also written `{x | p x}`) and membership of a set (`∈`) should be
used to convert between sets and predicates.

A **bornology** on a type `α` is a filter of cobounded sets which contains the cofinite filter.
Such spaces are equivalently specified by their bounded sets, see `Bornology.ofBounded`
and `Bornology.ext_iff_isBounded`
The cofinite filter is the filter of subsets whose complements are finite.

`Finset α` is the type of finite sets of elements of `α`. It is implemented
as a multiset (a list up to permutation) which has no duplicate elements.

`Multiset α` is the quotient of `List α` by list permutation. The result
is a type of finite sets with duplicates allowed.

Linked lists: ordered lists, in which each element has a reference to the next element.

Most operations on linked lists take time proportional to the length of the list, because each
element must be traversed to find the next element.

`List α` is isomorphic to `Array α`, but they are useful for different things:

Natural numbers less than some upper bound.

In particular, a `Fin n` is a natural number `i` with the constraint that `i < n`. It is the
canonical type with `n` elements.
Filter.atTop.{u_2} {α : Type u_2} [Preorder α] : Filter α

`atTop` is the filter representing the limit `→ ∞` on an ordered set.
It is generated by the collection of up-sets `{b | a ≤ b}`.
(The preorder need not have a top element for this to be well defined,
and indeed is trivial when a top element `x` exists, i.e., it coincides with `pure x`.)

A filter `F` on a type `α` is a collection of sets of `α` which contains the whole `α`,
is upwards-closed, and is stable under intersection. We do not forbid this collection to be
all sets of `α`.
Filter.Tendsto.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (f : α → β) (l₁ : Filter α) (l₂ : Filter β) : Prop

`Filter.Tendsto` is the generic "limit of a function" predicate.
`Tendsto f l₁ l₂` asserts that for every `l₂` neighborhood `a`,
the `f`-preimage of `a` is an `l₁` neighborhood.
A `Monoid` is a `Semigroup` with an element `1` such that `1 * a = a * 1 = a`.
A `Ring` is a `Semiring` with negation making it an additive group.

A `Field` is a `CommRing` with multiplicative inverses for nonzero elements.

An instance of `Field K` includes maps `ratCast : ℚ → K` and `qsmul : ℚ → K → K`.

This is a straightforward consequence of, and equivalent to, `Classical.choice`.

See also `choose_spec`, which asserts that the returned value has property `p`.

To create an existential proof, use the `exists` tactic,
or the anonymous constructor notation `⟨x, h⟩`.

`Or a b`, or `a ∨ b`, is the disjunction of propositions. There are two
constructors for `Or`, called `Or.inl : a → a ∨ b` and `Or.inr : b → a ∨ b`,
and you can use `match` or `cases` to destruct an `Or` assumption into the
two cases.

so if your goal is `¬p` you can use `intro h` to turn the goal into

and `(hn h).elim` will prove anything.

The `OfNat.ofNat` function is automatically inserted by the parser when
the user writes a numeric literal like `1 : α`. Implementations of this
typeclass can therefore customize the behavior of `n : α` based on `n` and
`α`.
Eq.symm.{u} {α : Sort u} {a b : α} (h : a = b) : b = a

Equality is symmetric: if `a = b` then `b = a`.

Because this is in the `Eq` namespace, if you have a variable `h : a = b`,
`h.symm` can be used as shorthand for `Eq.symm h` as a proof of `b = a`.

For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity

Eq.mpr.{u} {α β : Sort u} (h : α = β) (b : β) : α

If `h : α = β` is a proof of type equality, then `h.mpr : β → α` is the induced
"cast" operation in the reverse direction, mapping elements of `β` to elements of `α`.

You can prove theorems about the resulting element by induction on `h`, since
`rfl.mpr` is definitionally the identity function.

It represents a contradiction. `False` elimination rule, `False.rec`,
expresses the fact that anything follows from a contradiction.
This rule is sometimes called ex falso (short for ex falso sequitur quodlibet),
